concepts.subject: Data Structures
concepts.title: Why Dijkstra fails with negative edges
concepts.summary: The greedy "settled" set assumes no later path can improve a settled distance — negative edges break that invariant.
concepts.explanation: Dijkstra settles the closest unvisited node and never revisits it. That works because all remaining edges are non-negative, so a settled distance can never shrink later. With a negative edge, a longer-looking path can reduce a settled distance after all — the algorithm would have already locked in a wrong answer.
keyPoints: Settled nodes are never relaxed again
Negative edges can shorten settled distances
Bellman-Ford relaxes all edges V−1 times and handles negatives
concepts.example: Graph A→B (4), A→C (2), C→B (−3): Dijkstra picks B at 4 from A, but the true shortest A→C→B is −1.

concepts.subject: Networks
concepts.title: TCP congestion window vs receive window
concepts.summary: Congestion window is network-side flow control; receive window is receiver-side — the effective window is the minimum.
concepts.explanation: The sender may send up to min(cwnd, rwnd) unacknowledged bytes. cwnd adapts to network congestion (slow start, congestion avoidance, fast retransmit), while rwnd reflects the receiver's buffer capacity advertised in every ACK.
concepts.example: If cwnd = 8 segments and rwnd = 3, only 3 can be in flight — the receiver is the bottleneck.

concepts.subject: Chemistry
concepts.title: Why CO is a strong field ligand
concepts.summary: CO is a π-acceptor: it donates σ electron density but also accepts d-electron density back into its empty π* orbitals, raising Δo.
concepts.explanation: Ligand field strength depends on both σ donation and π back-bonding. CO's empty π* orbitals accept electron density from the metal, which stabilises the t2g set and increases the splitting energy Δo — making CO a strong-field ligand that favours low-spin complexes.
keyPoints: Synergic bonding: σ donation + π back-donation
concepts.example: [Co(CO)6]³⁺ is diamagnetic (low spin) because CO forces pairing.

concepts.subject: Mathematics
concepts.title: Definite integration by substitution — when to switch limits
concepts.summary: When you substitute u = g(x), the limits must change to u-values: ∫ₐᵇ f(g(x))g′(x)dx = ∫_{g(a)}^{g(b)} f(u)du.
concepts.explanation: The substitution theorem maps the x-interval to a u-interval. Forgetting to convert limits is the single most common exam error. If the function is odd/even, symmetry properties can shortcut the computation entirely.
keyPoints: Convert limits: u = g(a), u = g(b)
concepts.example: ∫₀^π sin²x·cos x dx with u = sin x: limits become 0 → 0? No — sin 0 = 0, sin π = 0, so the integral is 0.

concepts.subject: Operating Systems
concepts.title: Paging vs segmentation — the trade-off
concepts.summary: Paging splits memory into fixed frames (no external fragmentation, internal waste possible); segmentation splits by logical units (no internal waste, external fragmentation).
concepts.explanation: Paging uses fixed-size pages mapped through a page table — simple, no compaction needed, but a program's last page may be half empty. Segmentation divides memory by logical segments (code, data, stack) with base+limit — natural sharing and protection, but variable sizes cause external fragmentation.
keyPoints: Paging: fixed size, page table, internal fragmentation
Segmentation: logical units, base+limit, external fragmentation
concepts.example: A 70 KB program on 32 KB pages uses 3 frames: 2 full + 1 with 26 KB wasted (internal).

concepts.subject: Machine Learning
concepts.title: L1 vs L2 regularisation — why L1 gives sparse weights
concepts.summary: L1 penalises the absolute weight (diamond constraint) which hits corners → exact zeros; L2 penalises the square (sphere) → small but non-zero weights.
concepts.explanation: Both shrink weights toward zero, but the geometry differs. The L1 constraint region is a diamond whose corners lie on the axes — the optimal point often lands on a corner, zeroing some features. L2's spherical region rarely touches the axes, so weights shrink smoothly but stay non-zero.
keyPoints: L1 is non-differentiable at zero; L2 always differentiable
concepts.example: With two features, L1 optimisation often yields (w₁, 0) or (0, w₂); L2 yields (0.4, 0.7).

questions.q: Which algorithm finds shortest paths with negative edges (no negative cycles)?
questions.explanation: Bellman-Ford relaxes all edges V−1 times, handling negative weights.

questions.q: Time complexity of Dijkstra with a binary heap?
questions.explanation: Each extract-min is O(log V); total O((V+E) log V) ≈ O(E log V).

questions.q: A back-edge in DFS of a directed graph indicates…
questions.explanation: Back-edges point to an ancestor — exactly what forms a cycle.

questions.q: Kruskal's algorithm is best implemented with…
questions.explanation: Union-Find gives near-constant cycle checks while processing sorted edges.

questions.q: For a concave lens, the image formed by a real object is always…
questions.explanation: Concave lenses always form virtual, erect, diminished images.

questions.q: Lens maker's formula uses which convention for radii?
questions.explanation: New Cartesian: radii positive in the direction of incident light.

questions.q: A convex lens of power +2 D has focal length…
Critical angle exists only when light travels from…
questions.explanation: TIR needs a denser-to-rarer transition with angle > critical angle.

quizBank.q: Which data structure gives O(1) average lookup?
quizBank.explanation: Hash tables average O(1) per operation with good hashing.
Unlucky pivots (e.g., sorted input, first-element pivot) give O(n²).

quizBank.q: Which traversal uses a stack implicitly?
quizBank.explanation: DFS recursion uses the call stack; iterative DFS uses an explicit stack.

quizBank.q: A segment tree supports which queries in O(log n)?
quizBank.explanation: Range queries and point updates both run in O(log n).
Separate chaining and open addressing (linear/quadratic probing) are the two families.

options: V−1 relaxations then one more pass
quizBank.explanation: If any edge relaxes on the V-th pass, a negative cycle exists.

quizBank.q: Which of these is NOT O(n log n) in the worst case?
quizBank.explanation: Quicksort degrades to O(n²) with poor pivot choices (naive implementations).

quizBank.q: For a max-heap, extracting the max takes…
quizBank.explanation: Remove root, bubble the last element down — O(log n).

quizBank.q: Trie lookup complexity for a word of length k?
quizBank.explanation: Each character walks one level — O(k) regardless of dictionary size.
0/1 Knapsack decision is NP-complete; the listed others are polynomial.
